Q: Auto create table rows at the beginning of each day A:

You can use the MySQL Event Scheduler to automatically execute a query periodically. At the end of each day you can insert all the missing rows for that day.

Q: (1231) Variable 'time_zone' can't be set to the value of 'NULL' A:

time_zone is the name of a system variable, so set time_zone = <something> is trying to set that variable, not a column in your table. You're not allowed to set this variable to NULL

To make it set the table column in the trigger, use the syntax tablename.columnname. And in the case of a trigger you can use NEW as the table name, to refer to the column in the row being updated.

SET NEW.time_zone = CONCAT(IF(c_offset > 0, '+', '-'), TIME_FORMAT(MAKETIME(ABS(c_offset), 0, 0), '%H:%S'));

You should also investigate why the code for getting the new value of user.time_zone is returning NULL.

Q: Reading And Writing to MYSQL in AWS Glue A:

Please note that you have to provide a valid database URL, not a localhost. I believe your jupyter notebook was run locally on a laptop, in the same local environment where your mysql is running as well.

AWS Glue runs within an AWS environment, and behind the scene it would launch number of EC2 instances depending upon the DPU configuration. If your URL is configured as LOCALHOST, then the EC2 instance where the pyspark code is running, would look for a mysql database on the same node.

Please make sure you have a valid public IP for the mysql database, and try to setup a connection in the AWS Glue as suggested by bdcloud, and retry again. If you dont want to create a connection, you can hard code the connection parameters in the code and try again. If you cannot get a public IP for the installed mysql database, maybe you can try setup an RDS Mysql on AWS, and use it for testing.

Sample code snippet:

conn = mysql.connector.connect(host=url, user=uname, password=pwd, database=dbase)
cur = conn.cursor()

insertQry = "INSERT INTO emp (id, emp_name, dept, designation, address1, city, state, active_start_date, is_active) SELECT (SELECT coalesce(MAX(ID),0) + 1 FROM atlas.emp) id, tmp.emp_name, tmp.dept, tmp.designation, tmp.address1, tmp.city, tmp.state, tmp.active_start_date, tmp.is_active from EMP_STG tmp ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE dept=tmp.dept, designation=tmp.designation, address1=tmp.address1, city=tmp.city, state=tmp.state, active_start_date=tmp.active_start_date, is_active =tmp.is_active ;"

n = cur.execute(insertQry)
print (" CURSOR status :", n)

Q: com.hazelcast.core.HazelcastInstance IllegalStateException: Node failed to start A:

If there is another instance of your app running on localhost:5701, this would also cause this error.

In this case, in addition to the given workarounds, you might try to use another port instead of 5701 for your app.

Q: What does ZScaleInterval() do in AstroPy? A:

In the astropy.visualization context we think of an array (aka the values provided in the question) as an image, say z(x,y), that we want to visualize. Here x and y refer to the pixel coordinates (integers) while z (float) refers to the brightness or intensity value of a pixel. Visualization entails translating the pixel values to brightness values, b(z), that then can be used to look up a specific color in one of the many colormaps that exist for this purpoose (see, e.g., matplotlib colormaps or [cmasher colormaps]).

Conceptually, we may think of b being confined to the interval [0,+1], where 0 points to the leftmost or bottom value in the colormap (e.g., black in cmasher's neutral map) and +1 corresponds to the other extreme of the color map (e.g., white in cmasher's neutral map). Normalization of the image to brightness values requires us to choose an interval [vmin,vmax] in order to fix b(z ≤ vmin)=0 and b(z ≥ vmax)=+1. The functional form of the mapping b(z) for z ∈ [vmin, vmax] is called "stretch", with a linear stretch being the most simple form for b(z).

ZScaleInterval is used to obtain suitable vmin and vmax for the linear stretch, especially when working with raw-detector data. In raw detector data of imagers and spectrographs (e.g., CCDs in the optical) we often have to deal with a noise floor around a bias value with some small additive signal from the faint astronomical sources of interest. However the array will also contain high-valued artifacts (e.g., telluric lines in spectroscopic data and cosmic ray impacts overflowing some pixels). We deem a the intervall suitable when the resulting visualization with a sequential colormap allows to discern features of interest (sources) in the data easily by eye. We thus require the interval [vmin,vmax] to encircle the noise floor with an ideal dynamic range for a linear stretch.

Encircling the noise floor obviously is achieved by taking the median of the array as the center of the [vmin,vmax] interval. But how far should we go from the median in positive and negative direction to achieve an ideal contrast? The ZScaleIntervall algorithm finds a answer to this question in a unique, clever, and computationally efficient way. However, the latter seems to be less of a concern nowadays then it was even for 1k×1k CCDs in the 80ies.

The main outline of the algorithm can be summarized as follows:

  1. Take n_samples samples from the original array. In the astropy implementation this is achieved by "striding` through the array, i.e., by collecting z-values in regularly spaced intervals along the x- and y- axis. This speeds up things significantly, as from here only this subset of values from the original i mage is being considered.

  2. Sort the resulting array, say z' of n_samples samples, such that z'[0] = min(z'), z'[n_samples-1] = max(z'), and z'[(n_samples-1)/2] = median(z').

  3. Fit a line to the sorted array, z'[i] This fit is done iteratively with κ·σ-clipping algorithm. This makes the best-fit robust against non-linear tails (e.g., saturated pixel values, strong sky-lines in spectroscopic data, or other types of artifacts that lead to tails in the distribution of pixel values).

  4. Rescale the slope of the best-fit line by a contrast parameter c, with 0 < c < 1 (default: 0.25) while forcing this new line through the median. Read of the corresponding vmin and vmax of at the first and last index of the sorted array.

Graphically, the last step can be visualized as follows:

In this figure i_s refers to the indexes of the sorted sample of the array pixels of length n_samples (here n_pix). Moreover, the data is assumed to be well behaving, i.e. the best fit z(i_z) extrapolates well to values near min(z') and max(z'). The actual implementation contains several fixes against non-well behaving data.

Since code is always the best documentation, here is a link to a python version of the original IRAF implementation: https://github.com/spacetelescope/stsci.numdisplay/blob/master/lib/stsci/numdisplay/zscale.py
